skills.title: Observation
skills.summary: An observation is information gathered directly with your senses or instruments, without adding explanation.
objectives: Describe what you directly sense or measure
Tell an observation apart from an opinion

skills.title: Inference
skills.summary: An inference is a conclusion or explanation you reach by reasoning from observations — it goes beyond what you directly sense.
objectives: Distinguish an observation from an inference
Explain the reasoning behind an inference

skills.title: Testable Questions
skills.summary: A testable question can be answered by gathering evidence through observation or experiment.
objectives: Rewrite an untestable question so it can be tested

skills.title: Hypotheses
skills.summary: A hypothesis is a testable, reasoned prediction about what will happen and why.
objectives: State a hypothesis as a testable prediction with a reason
Tell a hypothesis apart from a guess

skills.title: Evidence and Conclusions
skills.summary: Evidence is data that supports or challenges a claim. A conclusion follows from evidence, and correlation does not prove causation.
objectives: Use evidence to support or challenge a claim
Explain why correlation does not always mean causation

skills.title: Scientific Models
skills.summary: A scientific model is a simplified representation of something real - a diagram, a physical replica, an equation, or a simulation - used to explain and predict. Models leave out detail on purpose, so every model has limits.
objectives: Explain what a scientific model is for.
State a limitation of a given model.

skills.title: Scientific Explanations
skills.summary: A scientific explanation states a claim, supports it with evidence, and gives reasoning that links the two. It differs from an opinion because it can be checked against data, and it must account for the observations rather than restate them.
objectives: State the parts of a scientific explanation.
Distinguish an explanation from an opinion.
Judge whether an explanation is supported by evidence.

components.body: Describe what you directly sense or measure, without adding explanation.
An observation is what you can see, hear, feel, smell, or measure right now. 'The ground is wet' is an observation. Saying 'it rained' is not — that is a guess about the cause.
An observation records information from the senses or an instrument. It does not include why something happened.
Looking at a plant: 'The leaves are yellow' is an observation. 'The plant is sick' is not — that is an explanation you added.
Adding a cause or opinion turns an observation into something else. Keep observations to what you directly detect.
Observation = what you directly sense or measure, with no explanation attached.
Reach a reasoned conclusion from observations and label it as an inference.
An observation is what you directly sense. An inference goes one step further.
If you observe wet ground and puddles, you might infer that it rained. The inference is your explanation — it could be wrong (a sprinkler may have run).
Observation: 'The window is broken and there is a ball inside.' Inference: 'A ball broke the window.' The inference explains the observations but is not something you directly saw.
Inference = a conclusion reasoned from observations; it may be wrong and needs evidence.
Recognize questions that can be answered by gathering evidence.
A testable question can be answered by observing or experimenting. 'Does more water make a plant grow taller?' is testable. 'Are roses the best flower?' is not — it is an opinion.
Turn 'Is music good?' into a testable question: 'Do students score higher on a memory test with music or with silence?'
Testable question = one you can answer with observation or experiment, not opinion.
Write a hypothesis as a testable prediction with a reason.
A hypothesis predicts what will happen and gives a reason. It is more than a guess because it can be tested and explained.
A common form is: 'If [change], then [predicted result], because [reason].'
'If a plant gets more sunlight, then it will grow taller, because sunlight provides energy for growth.' This is testable and gives a reason.
Hypothesis = a testable prediction with a reason, not just a guess.
Use evidence to support a conclusion, and avoid confusing correlation with causation.
Evidence is data that supports or challenges a claim. A conclusion should follow from the evidence — not from what you hoped to find.
Two things that rise and fall together are correlated. Correlation does not prove that one causes the other; a third factor may cause both.
Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer. They are correlated, but ice cream does not cause sunburn — hot, sunny weather raises both.
Do not assume that because two things happen together, one causes the other.
Evidence supports conclusions; correlation alone does not prove causation.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to say what a scientific model is, give examples, and describe limits of a model.
Recall that an inference is an explanation you reason out from observations. Models are tools that help you make and test such explanations.

A map is a model of a city. It is not the city: it leaves out most buildings, colors, and people. But because it keeps the parts you need, it helps you predict which streets connect. Scientific models work the same way, keeping the important parts and dropping the rest.

A scientific model is a simplified representation of an object, system, or process, used to explain observations and predict what will happen. Models can be physical, diagrammatic, mathematical, or computational. Because a model simplifies, it always has limitations and can be revised as evidence improves.
A globe models the Earth: it shows shape and the arrangement of continents accurately, but it is far smaller, cannot show weather, and its painted colors are not real surface colors.

Is a diagram of the water cycle a model? Yes. It represents a real process in simplified form, using arrows for evaporation and rainfall so you can explain and predict where water goes. It leaves out the vast detail of real weather.
Name a limitation of a globe as a model of Earth. It is not to full scale and cannot show changing features such as clouds or seasons.
A common mistake is treating a model as a perfect copy of reality. Models simplify on purpose; being incomplete is expected, not a flaw, but it does limit what the model can tell you.
A scientific model is a simplified representation used to explain and predict. Models can be physical, diagrammatic, or mathematical, and every model has limits because it leaves detail out.
What is a scientific model for, and why does every model have limitations?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to build and judge a scientific explanation using claim, evidence, and reasoning.
Recall that evidence is data that supports or challenges an idea, and that models help explain how something works.

Saying 'the plant died because I forgot to water it' is an explanation only if you can point to something you observed, like dry soil and wilted leaves, and say why that would cause death. A claim on its own is just an assertion; evidence and reasoning turn it into science.

A scientific explanation has three parts: a claim (a statement answering the question), evidence (data or observations that support the claim), and reasoning (why the evidence supports the claim, often using a scientific principle). A good explanation accounts for the observations and can be tested against new data.

Question: why did the ice melt faster on the metal tray? Claim: metal transfers heat to the ice faster than plastic. Evidence: ice on metal melted in 4 minutes; ice on plastic took 11 minutes. Reasoning: metal conducts heat well, so it moves energy into the ice more quickly.

Which part is missing here: 'The plant grew taller because it got more light. It grew 12 cm versus 4 cm.' The claim and evidence are present, so the missing part is the reasoning linking light to growth.

A common mistake is restating the observation instead of explaining it ('it melted because it got warmer'), or giving a claim with no evidence. Explanations must connect evidence to the claim with reasoning.
A scientific explanation combines a claim, supporting evidence, and reasoning that links them. It must account for the observations and be testable, unlike an opinion.
What are the three parts of a scientific explanation, and what does the reasoning part do?

questions.prompt: Which statement is an observation?

answer_spec.correct_answer: The ground is wet

hints.text: An observation is something you can directly sense right now.
The other choices explain a cause you did not directly see.

questions.explanation: You can directly see that the ground is wet. The other statements add an explanation, so they are inferences.

questions.prompt: An observation should describe...

options: what you directly sense or measure

answer_spec.correct_answer: what you directly sense or measure

hints.text: Observations do not include explanations.

questions.explanation: An observation records what your senses or instruments detect, with no explanation added.

questions.prompt: You see wet ground and puddles. Which statement is an inference?

answer_spec.correct_answer: It rained recently

hints.text: An inference is a conclusion you reason to, not something you directly see.

questions.explanation: 'It rained recently' is a conclusion reasoned from the observations; the others are the observations themselves.

questions.prompt: How is an inference different from an observation?

options: It adds reasoning that goes beyond what you sense

answer_spec.correct_answer: It adds reasoning that goes beyond what you sense

hints.text: Inferences can be wrong; observations are what you detect.

questions.explanation: An inference reasons beyond the direct observation, so it can be wrong and needs evidence.

questions.prompt: Which question can be tested with an experiment?

options: Does more sunlight make plants grow taller?

answer_spec.correct_answer: Does more sunlight make plants grow taller?

hints.text: A testable question can be answered by gathering evidence.

questions.explanation: You can measure plant height under different amounts of sunlight. The others are opinions.

questions.prompt: Which is the best hypothesis?

options: If a plant gets more sunlight, it will grow taller, because sunlight gives energy for growth
I think the plant will do something

answer_spec.correct_answer: If a plant gets more sunlight, it will grow taller, because sunlight gives energy for growth

hints.text: A hypothesis is a testable prediction with a reason.

questions.explanation: A good hypothesis predicts a result and gives a reason, and it can be tested.

questions.prompt: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer. What is the best conclusion?

options: They are correlated, but one may not cause the other
Sunburns cause people to buy ice cream

answer_spec.correct_answer: They are correlated, but one may not cause the other

hints.text: Two things rising together does not prove one causes the other.
Hot, sunny weather could raise both.

questions.explanation: The two are correlated, but a third factor (hot, sunny weather) likely drives both — correlation is not causation.

questions.prompt: Evidence is best described as...

options: data that supports or challenges a claim
an opinion you feel strongly about

answer_spec.correct_answer: data that supports or challenges a claim

hints.text: Evidence comes from observation or measurement.

questions.explanation: Evidence is data that supports or challenges a claim, letting you judge it fairly.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of a simple investigation in order.

options: Run a test and gather evidence

correct_answer: Run a test and gather evidence

hints.text: You notice something before you can ask about it.
A hypothesis comes after the question and before the test.

questions.explanation: You observe, then ask a testable question, then form a hypothesis, then test it to gather evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a scientific model?

answer_spec.correct_answer: to explain and predict

hints.text: Think about what a map lets you do.
Models help you understand and forecast.

questions.explanation: A scientific model represents something in simplified form so you can explain observations and predict outcomes.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of a scientific model?

answer_spec.correct_answer: a diagram of the water cycle

hints.text: A model represents a real system in simplified form.
A labelled diagram of a process qualifies.

questions.explanation: A water-cycle diagram represents a real process in simplified form, so it is a model.

options: a diagram of the water cycle

questions.prompt: A globe is a model of Earth. What is one limitation?

answer_spec.correct_answer: it is not full size and cannot show changing weather

hints.text: Models leave detail out.
Think about scale and what a globe cannot display.

questions.explanation: A globe simplifies: it is far smaller than Earth and cannot show changing features such as weather.

options: it is not full size and cannot show changing weather

questions.prompt: True or false: a good model must include every detail of the real thing.

answer_spec.correct_answer: False

hints.text: Models simplify on purpose.
Including every detail would make a model useless.

questions.explanation: Models deliberately leave out detail; simplification is what makes them useful.

questions.prompt: Select every item that is a scientific model.

hints.text: A model represents a system in simplified form.
Physical, mathematical, and computational representations all count.

questions.explanation: A globe, an equation, and a simulation all represent real systems in simplified form; a thermometer and a raw data table are tools and records, not models.

questions.prompt: New evidence contradicts part of a model. What should scientists do?

answer_spec.correct_answer: revise the model

hints.text: Models are not fixed truths.
Evidence drives changes to models.

questions.explanation: Models are revised when evidence contradicts them; that is how scientific understanding improves.

questions.prompt: A model airplane in a wind tunnel is used to study a real aircraft. Why use a model?

answer_spec.correct_answer: it is safer and cheaper to test than the real aircraft

hints.text: Consider cost and risk.
Models let you test without the real thing.

questions.explanation: A scale model lets researchers test behavior safely and cheaply before building the real aircraft.

options: it is safer and cheaper to test than the real aircraft
it removes the need for data

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a mathematical model?

answer_spec.correct_answer: an equation that describes how quantities relate

hints.text: Mathematical models use numbers and symbols.
They capture relationships between quantities.

questions.explanation: A mathematical model uses an equation to describe how quantities relate, letting you predict values.

options: an equation that describes how quantities relate

questions.prompt: What are the three parts of a scientific explanation?

answer_spec.correct_answer: claim, evidence, and reasoning

hints.text: One part states the answer, one supports it, one links them.
Claim, evidence, reasoning.

questions.explanation: A scientific explanation states a claim, gives evidence, and provides reasoning connecting them.

questions.prompt: What makes a scientific explanation different from an opinion?

answer_spec.correct_answer: it is supported by evidence and can be tested

hints.text: Opinions need no data.
Explanations must stand up to evidence.

questions.explanation: A scientific explanation is backed by evidence and can be checked against data; an opinion need not be.

options: it is supported by evidence and can be tested

questions.prompt: 'The plant grew taller because it got more light. It grew 12 cm versus 4 cm.' Which part is missing?

answer_spec.correct_answer: reasoning

hints.text: A claim and evidence are both present.
Nothing explains why light causes growth.

questions.explanation: The claim and evidence are present, but the reasoning linking light to plant growth is missing.

questions.prompt: Which is the weakest scientific explanation?

answer_spec.correct_answer: The ice melted because it stopped being frozen.

hints.text: Look for one that just restates the observation.
Restating is not explaining.

questions.explanation: Saying ice melted because it stopped being frozen restates the observation instead of explaining a cause.

options: The ice melted because it stopped being frozen.
The ice melted faster on metal because metal conducts heat well.
The plant grew more in light because light powers photosynthesis.
The ball rolled farther on tile because tile has less friction.

common_wrong_answers.value: The ice melted because it stopped being frozen.

questions.prompt: An explanation contradicts the collected data. What should you do?

answer_spec.correct_answer: revise the explanation to fit the evidence

hints.text: Evidence has priority.
Change the explanation, not the data.

questions.explanation: When data contradicts an explanation, the explanation must be revised; you never adjust evidence to fit.

options: revise the explanation to fit the evidence

questions.prompt: In a scientific explanation, what is the role of evidence?

answer_spec.correct_answer: to support the claim with observations or data

hints.text: Evidence is what you actually measured or saw.
It backs the claim.

questions.explanation: Evidence supplies the observations or data that support the claim.

options: to support the claim with observations or data

questions.prompt: Select every statement that is a claim rather than evidence.

correct_answer: Metal transfers heat faster than plastic
The plant needs light to grow

hints.text: A claim is a statement being argued for.
Evidence is a specific measurement or observation.

questions.explanation: The two general statements are claims; the measured times and heights are evidence.

options: Metal transfers heat faster than plastic
Ice on metal melted in 4 minutes
The plant needs light to grow
The plant grew 12 cm in two weeks

questions.prompt: Why must a scientific explanation be testable?

answer_spec.correct_answer: so others can check it against new evidence

hints.text: Science relies on independent checking.
Untestable claims cannot be confirmed or refuted.

questions.explanation: Testability lets others gather new evidence to confirm or refute the explanation.

options: so others can check it against new evidence
so it can never be wrong
